title: What Biblical Theology Is and Why Every Teacher Needs It
subtitle: An introduction to biblical theology and the single storyline of Scripture from Genesis to Revelation, and why every preacher and Bible teacher needs it

sections.title: The Bible Is One Story, Not Sixty-Six
sections.body:
Most of us were handed the Bible as a collection. Sixty-six books, written by dozens of hands across many centuries, useful for verses and lessons and the occasional argument. A reference manual with a leather cover.

It is not a collection. It is a story.

Biblical theology is the discipline of reading Scripture as the single, unfolding account it claims to be, one narrative that runs from a garden in Genesis to a city in Revelation, with one author behind the many and one redemption being worked out from beginning to end. This is not a clever overlay we impose on the text. It is the shape the text already has, the through line the writers themselves kept pointing at. To miss it is to read every chapter as a fragment. To see it is to watch the fragments become a face.

sections.title: How It Differs From Systematic Theology
sections.body:
Biblical theology is not the same as systematic theology, and a teacher needs both. Systematic theology gathers everything the whole Bible teaches on a topic and arranges it by subject: the doctrine of God, of sin, of salvation. It asks what is true.

Biblical theology asks a different question. It asks how the story got here. It follows themes as they grow across the timeline, watching how an idea begins as a seed in the early pages and ripens through the prophets and flowers in Christ.

Take the theme of the temple. Systematic theology will tell you what God's presence means. Biblical theology will walk you from the garden where God walked with man, to the tabernacle in the wilderness, to Solomon's stone temple, to the man who said destroy this temple and I will raise it in three days, to the church as a temple of the Spirit, to the city at the end where there is no temple because God himself is its temple. Same God, one story, traced through time. You need the system to know what is true. You need the story to know what God was doing.

sections.title: Creation, Fall, Redemption, Restoration
sections.body:
The story has a spine, and once you see it you cannot stop seeing it. It moves in four movements.

Creation: God makes a good world and places his image bearers in it to know him and reflect him. Fall: they rebel, and the ruin spreads into every relationship and every cell of the world. Redemption: God refuses to abandon what he made and works through a man, a family, a nation, and finally his own Son to buy it back. Restoration: he makes all things new, not a return to the garden but the arrival of the city, the project finished.

Every passage of the Bible sits somewhere on that arc, and knowing where changes how you read it. The law assumes the fall. The prophets ache toward redemption. The Gospels announce its arrival. Read any text as part of that four movement story and it stops being a stranded fragment and starts pulling its weight in something vast.

sections.title: Every Road Leads to the One Who Walked the Emmaus Road
sections.body:
There is a center to this story, and he told us so himself. On the road to Emmaus, the risen Jesus took two heartbroken disciples through the whole of the Old Testament and showed them how it all spoke of him.

That is the claim biblical theology takes seriously. The Old Testament is not a separate religion stapled to the front of the New. It is the setup, the promise, the long shadow cast by a person who had not yet stepped into the light.

This is why a teacher who knows biblical theology preaches Christ from the whole Bible without forcing him into every verse by cheap tricks. He does not have to invent Jesus in the text. He follows the lines the authors drew and finds that they were always heading somewhere, that the sacrifices and the kings and the exile and the return were a story leaning forward, waiting. Not a verse here and there about Jesus. A whole testament bending toward him.

sections.title: Why the Teacher Who Lacks It Will Mislead
sections.body:
A teacher without biblical theology is not neutral. He is a teacher who will, sooner or later, mishandle the text, because he is reading parts without the whole that gives them meaning.

He will preach the conquest of Canaan as a manual for crushing his enemies, having missed that it sits inside a story heading toward a cross where the King dies for his enemies. He will turn David and Goliath into a pep talk about facing your giants, having missed that the point was a champion who fights the battle his people cannot fight. He will moralize the Old Testament into a series of good examples and bad ones, and starve his people of the gospel that runs underneath all of it.

This is not a luxury for scholars. It is the difference between feeding people and confusing them. Learn the one story. Find where each text lives inside it. Then you will not have to manufacture meaning, because you will finally be reading the Bible the way it was written, as a single word about a single Savior, from the garden to the city, and nothing in between left out.
